justice: Most of the visible space is allocated to a wide asphalt carriageway, while pedestrian space is minimal and discontinuous, indicating an uneven distribution of street resources among road users.

A narrow sidewalk appears only along the left building edge, and there is no clearly defined pedestrian path on the right side next to the fence and planting strip, which limits equal access for people moving on foot.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free elements can be identified in the scene, so accessibility support for diverse users is weak.
safety: Motor vehicles and pedestrians appear to share the same open paved area because there are no visible bollards, raised sidewalks, or protective barriers separating walking space from the roadway.
The road is relatively wide and visually open, which can help sightlines, but there are no marked crossings, warning signs, or traffic-calming features visible near the bend and driveway-like space.
Some greenery and a fence line the right edge, yet the area feels lightly supervised with few active frontages or visible people, which may reduce perceived personal safety.
livability: The scene is dominated by service-road asphalt, fenced edges, and blank building sides rather than active storefronts, seating, or community-oriented amenities, which weakens everyday street life.
There are planted shrubs and several trees near the center and right side, but they function more as edge landscaping than as usable social or recreational space.
No benches, bus stops, kiosks, or visible gathering places are present, so the street offers limited support for lingering, social interaction, or daily convenience.
sustainability: The presence of trees, shrubs, and a planted verge on the right adds some green infrastructure and modest ecological value compared with a fully paved environment.
However, the street remains heavily asphalted, and no visible permeable paving, bioswales, rain gardens, or stormwater features can be identified.
There is no visible bike lane, transit stop, or other clear low-carbon mobility facility, so support for sustainable travel modes appears limited.
aesthetics: The trees and planted beds soften the scene and provide some visual relief against the large paved surface and building masses.
Building forms are simple and fairly orderly, but the environment lacks distinctive facade detail, active edges, or cohesive streetscape design elements.
Patchy asphalt stains, exposed fencing, and a utilitarian service-road character reduce visual quality despite the relatively clean and uncluttered appearance.
comfort: Several trees provide limited shade in the middle distance, but most of the roadway and walking edges are exposed to direct sun, reducing thermal comfort in hot weather.
The visible pedestrian surface is narrow and inconsistent, and there are no benches or resting facilities, which lowers physical comfort for people moving through the space.
Low traffic volume may reduce noise and stress, but the sparse activity, open asphalt expanse, and lack of dedicated pedestrian refuge can make the environment feel psychologically less comfortable.
walkability: Continuous sidewalks are not clearly provided on both sides of the street; the left side has only a narrow edge path and the right side lacks a defined pedestrian walkway.
No marked crosswalks, curb ramps, pedestrian signs, or intersection treatments are visible, which weakens route continuity and safe pedestrian movement.
Although the street appears relatively flat and lightly trafficked, the dominance of vehicle pavement over pedestrian infrastructure makes walking feel secondary rather than prioritized.
